caseNote: 가상 사례 (레스토랑 단체 예약, 소프트웨어 갱신, 식자재 납품) + 일화 (Getting to Yes에 나오는 도서관 창문 이야기)
insight: 상대가 고집하는 숫자나 요구는 답 하나일 뿐이다. 그 뒤에 숨은 이유를 찾으면 다른 답이 보인다.
misconception: 협상은 상대가 내건 숫자를 두고 누가 더 버티느냐의 싸움이다. 중간에서 나누는 것이 가장 공정한 해결이다.

sources.text: Fisher, R., & Ury, W. (1981). Getting to Yes: Negotiating Agreement Without Giving In. Houghton Mifflin. (입장 대신 이해관계에 집중하라는 원칙, 도서관 창문 이야기)
Mary Parker Follett, 협상과 갈등에 관한 1920년대 글 (도서관 창문 이야기의 원출처로 알려짐)
레스토랑, 소프트웨어, 식자재 납품 사례와 수치는 모두 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 도서관 창문 이야기가 Getting to Yes(1981)에 나오고 Mary Parker Follett에게서 빌려 온 이야기로 소개되는지 원문에서 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 연구가 아닌 '가르치기 위한 이야기'로 표시했습니다.
레스토랑 계산: 예산 $2,000 ÷ 40명 = 1인당 $50. 메뉴 가격 $65는 가정입니다.
소프트웨어 계산: 40석 → 28석 = 28 ÷ 40 = 0.7, 청구액 30% 감소. 좌석당 가격은 그대로라는 가정입니다. 사용 좌석 26석은 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: Two deals stuck on one number
body: A restaurant and a software company are in the same spot this week. A customer has named a number and won't move.
Both sellers are about to make the same mistake: arguing about the number.

image.label: Two sellers facing customers who hold up a single number
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 3D 클레이 일러스트. 왼쪽은 레스토랑 매니저와 "$50" 팻말을 든 손님, 오른쪽은 노트북 앞 영업 담당자와 "-30%" 팻말을 든 고객. 양쪽 모두 팽팽하게 마주 선 분위기. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The party that wants $50 a head.
body: You run a restaurant. A company wants your private room for 40 guests on a Saturday. Your set menu is $65 a head.
The organizer says: "$50 a head, or we book elsewhere." Saturday is your busiest night. What's your first move?

options.feedback: Quick and polite, and many deals end this way. But you give up margin without learning anything, and $57 may still not work for her.

options.text: Hold at $65 and explain your costs
options.feedback: You protect your price but turn the talk into a contest of wills. If $50 is a hard limit, you lose the booking without knowing why.
It costs you one question, and it may open a deal at a price you can accept. That's the idea in this lesson.

cards.title: Behind the number was a budget line.
body: The organizer explained. Her company approved **$2,000** for the event, and she can't go over it. $2,000 for 40 people is $50 each. She cares less about Saturday than about staying on budget and not looking cheap in front of her team.
Now there's room to move. A Thursday night, when your room usually sits empty, with a shorter three-course menu, fits her budget and your costs. Neither of you had to win the number.

cards.title: Positions vs interests
body: A **position** is what someone says they want: "$50 a head." An **interest** is why they want it: a fixed budget, a deadline, a fear of looking bad.
Positions are usually fixed. Interests can often be met in more than one way. Arguing over positions turns a deal into a tug-of-war. Asking about interests turns it into a shared problem.

image.label: An iceberg: the position above water, interests below
image.brief: 빙산 인포그래픽. 물 위의 작은 부분에 "Position: $50 a head", 물 아래의 큰 부분에 "Fixed budget", "Look good to my team", "Any night is fine" 라벨. 물 아래 부분이 훨씬 크게 보이도록.

cards.title: An old story about a window.
body: Roger Fisher and William Ury made this idea famous in their 1981 book *Getting to Yes*. They retell a story, credited to management writer Mary Parker Follett, about two men arguing in a library. One wants the window open. The other wants it shut.

The librarian asks each one why. One wants fresh air. The other wants to avoid a draft. She opens a window in the next room. It's a teaching story, not a study, but the pattern shows up in real deals every day.

cards.title: The same move in software.
body: A software company hears from a 40-seat customer: "30% off at renewal, or we cancel." The rep could fight over the discount. Instead, she asks what's driving it.
The finance chief has been told to cut software spending, and only 26 of the 40 seats are used. The interest is a **smaller bill**, not a lower price per seat.
Dropping to 28 seats cuts the bill by 30%. Revenue falls either way, but the price per seat stays intact, and the customer trusts she isn't paying for empty seats.

image.label: 40 seats, 14 of them empty, shrinking to 28
image.brief: 좌석 아이콘 40개 중 14개가 회색(빈 좌석)으로 표시된 그림에서 화살표를 따라 28개로 줄어드는 모습. 옆에 "Bill −30%", "Price per seat: unchanged" 라벨. 실제 소프트웨어 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Questions that surface interests
body: Interests rarely come out on their own. A few questions help:
list: "What happens if you don't get it?"
"What would a good outcome look like for you?"
Then ask yourself: what is *your* number protecting?
cards.callout: Listen for budgets, deadlines, risks and reputations. Those are interests.

cards.title: Interests don't make every conflict disappear.
body: Some interests really do clash. If both sides simply want more money, no clever question removes that. You still need to know your alternatives and your limits.
Asking "why" can also sound like a challenge. Ask with curiosity, and share one of your own interests first. People don't always say what they truly need, so check what you hear against what they do.

cards.title: Now it's a food distributor.
body: You supply a small grocery store twice a week. The owner demands daily deliveries, which would cost more than the account earns.
You ask why. Her fresh herbs and salad leaves run out by Thursday, and her back room is too small to hold more. Which offer best serves her interest?

options.text: Agree to daily deliveries to keep her
options.feedback: You keep the customer, but you meet her position at a loss. Her real problem is two products, not every product.
A discount is pleasant, but her shelves are still empty on Thursday. She may move to a supplier who fixes that.

options.text: Add a small Thursday top-up of herbs and salad leaves only
options.feedback: It closes the gap that matters to her at a fraction of the cost of daily runs. You met the interest, not the position.

cards.title: Ask what the number is protecting.
body: A position is one answer to a problem. Find the problem, and there are usually other answers.
**Try it today:** pick a deal or request that's stuck. Write the other side's position, then three interests that might sit behind it. Choose one question to test them.
